Saptarshi,

On Apr 5, 2009, at 2:54 PM, Saptarshi Guha wrote:

>
> Hello,
>
>
> Can you, please, send me the exact code you're using? (I.e. exactly  
> the value of CLASSPATH, your platform, how you started R and  
> initialized rJava and what you tried to do to load the class).
>
> Platform is RH Enterprise Linux 5 on Intel. Started R from  
> commandline as  R.
>
> ==Code==
> library(rJava)
> .jinit();

^- this is the first problem as I mentioned in the previous e-mail -  
you should make sure that CLASSPATH is empty and use the classpath  
argument of the .jinit function instead. The difference is subtle but  
fatal in your case - see below.


>
> cfg <- .jnew("org/apache/hadoop/conf/Configuration")
> path1 <- .jnew("org/apache/hadoop/fs/ 
> Path",paste(Sys.getenv("HADOOP_CONF_DIR"),"/hadoop- 
> default.xml",sep=""))
> path2 <- .jnew("org/apache/hadoop/fs/ 
> Path",paste(Sys.getenv("HADOOP_CONF_DIR"),"/hadoop-site.xml",sep=""))
> .jcall(cfg,"V","addResource", path1)
> .jcall(cfg,"V","addResource", path2)
> .jcall("org/apache/hadoop/fs/FileSystem","Lorg/apache/hadoop/fs/ 
> FileSystem;","get",cfg)
> filesystem = FileSystem.get(config);
> ##filesystem is NULL
> .jgetEx()
> [1] "Java-Object{java.lang.RuntimeException:  
> java.lang.ClassNotFoundException:  
> org.apache.hadoop.hdfs.DistributedFileSystem}"
>
> All the above classes, including the one not found are in  
> hadoop-0.19.2-dev-core.jar.
> Strangley, cfg,path1,path2 are not null.  I also tried passing a   
> vector of the jar files to classpath jar files to .jinit but still  
> got the same result.
> Yet when I create the JVM (as I described), then I I dont get the  
> class not found error.
>
> Quickly looking through the hadoop sources, it does do some sort of  
> reflection  - does that have any bearing?
>

Yes. Usually Java code queries the class loader of the invoking class  
(i.e. the loader by which the class was loaded). Therefore if you use  
reflection in your code, it becomes crucial to have the right class  
loader. First problem is if really bad code attempts to use the  
bootstrap or system loader directly - that it completely wrong and  
won't work (hopefully that's not the case here, but I didn't check  
hadoop sources). Second problem arises when you set the system loader  
to find some of your classes - e.g. via CLASSPATH. The problem is that  
you make it possible for your classes to be loaded by the system  
loader instead of the rJava loader. Consequently those classes will  
use the wrong loader for reflection and thus won't find classes. As  
long as you don't use reflection (and don't load further packages that  
may use the same classes) everything may appear to work, but it's  
going through the wrong loader.

rJava uses its own loader because the Java system loader does not  
allow changes to the class path. However, in R we need to sequentially  
modify the class path as we load R packages using Java. Unfortunately  
Java does not allow full replacement of class loaders, it enforces a  
hierarchy that cannot be changed and the first two loaders are always  
the bootstrap and system loader. Therefore it is important to not let  
those loaders see any of your classes, otherwise they will bypass the  
rJava loader. If you use rJava as recommended, all is well, because  
the system and boot loaders will have an empty class path, so all  
control is in rJava. However, when you set CLASSPATH you will change  
that as described above.

I hope this makes the potential issue clearer. Please do as I  
recommended in the last e-mail (unset CLASSPATH and use classpath  
parameter of .jinit) and let me know if the problem persists.

Cheers,
Simon


> Thank you
> Saptarshi

Hmm.. I'm pretty sure that the issue is with hadoop picking up the  
wrong loader - one way or the other*. Chances are that they may be  
also providing their own loader or some class path manipulation and  
they don't ask the parent loader. If you are willing to modify their  
code, it should always ask the loader of the class which should be  
RJavaClassLoader (as an ultima ratio you can always get the loader  
via .jclassLoader() in R or RJavaClassLoader.getPrimaryLoader() in  
Java but it should not be necessary). If they are performing some  
magic classpath manipulation then it may be really nasty since that is  
effectively circumvention of the Java facilities. Let me know what you  
find out or if you need help with that.

* - actually, you can enable debugging messages in the rJava loader to  
see if it gets queried at all:
.jinit(..)
#...
cl=.jclassLoader()
cl$verbose=TRUE

then you should see something like:
 > a=.jnew("Test")
RJavaClassLoaaer.findClass("Test")
  - trying class path "/Users/urbanek/Library/R/2.8/library/rJava/java"
  - trying class path "."
RJavaClassLoader: loaded class Test, 253 bytes

Thanks,
Simon

BTW: I could add an option to .jinit that forces the system class path  
in the way you did manually for hard cases like this. It would be a  
hack that can cause trouble if you don't know what you're doing, but  
it could work around code that requires special class path handling  
like hadoop. The other limitation is that this can only be used as the  
first R package since you have to initialize JVM in a special way  
which won't work if another R package has initialized Java before  
(which is why we use the special loader).

> A side note - preferably you should not be using the CLASSPATH  
> environment variable, because that is very limited and doesn't work  
> if you have multiple packages using Java. Instead use .jinit  
> or .jpackage (under the hood CLASSPATH gets converted but that is  
> for compatibility only).
>
>
>
> Now If if, create my own vm (see below), and then run .jinit (which  
> will use my vm), i can find the class in question  
> (org.apache.hadoop.io.longwritable)
>
> Is there some classloader problem in rJava?
>
>
> No, more likely that your code is using the wrong class loader for  
> loading files. The code below sets the path in the system class  
> loader but that is not the loader used by R code. Since R needs to  
> modify the class path on the fly (as packages are loaded) it uses  
> its own class loader. It seems as if you are bypassing that loader  
> and thus running into problems (without exact details we can't tell  
> for sure).
>
> Cheers,
> Simon
>
>
>

> void create_vm(const char *clap) {
>  char* classpath = (char*) calloc(18+strlen(clap)+1, sizeof(char));

>  JavaVMInitArgs args;
>  JavaVMOption options[2];
>  args.version = JNI_VERSION_1_4;
>  args.nOptions = 2;
>  options[0].optionString = classpath;
>  options[1].optionString = "-Xrs";
>  args.options = options;
>  args.ignoreUnrecognized = JNI_TRUE;
>  JavaVM *jvms[32];
>  jsize vms=0;
>  int r=0;
>  r=JNI_GetCreatedJavaVMs(jvms, 32, &vms);
>  if (r) {
>  error("JNI_GetCreatedJavaVMs returned %d\n", r);
>  } else {
>  if (vms>0) {
>    int i=0;
>    while (i<vms) {
>  if (jvms[i]) {
>    if (!(*jvms[i])->AttachCurrentThread(jvms[i], (void**)&jenv,  
> NULL)) {
>      jvm=jvms[i];
>      break;
>    }
>  }
>  i++;
>    }
>    if (i==vms) error("Failed to attach to any existing JVM.");
>  }else {
>      JNI_CreateJavaVM(&jvm, (void **)&jenv, &args);
>    }
>  }
>  }

On Apr 28, 2009, at 14:54 , David Swartz wrote:

> I am running rJava 0.6-2 with R 2.8.1 on Mac OS X 10.5.6 on Intel. I
> am trying to figure out how to use the server JVM instead of the
> client JVM. I have tried specifying this in the .jinit function call:
>
> library(rJava)
> .jinit(parameters=c("-Xms100m","-Xmx612m","-server"))
> .jcall("java/lang/System", "S", "getProperty", "java.vm.name")
> [1] "Java HotSpot(TM) Client VM"
> .jcall("java/lang/System", "S", "getProperty", "java.version")
> [1] "1.5.0_16"
>

Apple does not support server VM in 32-bit. You have to run 64-bit R  
in order to be able to use the server VM:

 > R.version$platform
[1] "x86_64-apple-darwin9.6.0"
 > .jinit(parameters=c("-Xms100m","-Xmx612m","-server"))
 > .jcall("java/lang/System", "S", "getProperty", "java.vm.name")
[1] "Java HotSpot(TM) 64-Bit Server VM"

Cheers,
Simon

messages.body_plain:
This and several other questions I've seen roll by make me wonder why 
Apple is so far behind the curve in its Java capabilities.  Most 
notably, Java 1.6 is available only for 64-buit Macs.  32-bit Macs are 
stuck with 1.5 (aka J2SE 5.0).  Meanwhile, in java.sun.com, one reads:

> J2SE 5.0 is in its Java Technology End of Life (EOL) transition period. The EOL transition period began April 8th, 2008 and will complete October 30th, 2009, when J2SE 5.0 will have reached its End of Service Life (EOSL).

which suggests that Java 1.6 (aka J2SE 6.0) really should have been 
phased-in for all Macs at least a year ago.  Why is this?  And is it 
possible to build a Java 1.6 SDK from sources so that 32-bit Mac users 
can be up-to-date?
--
